query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A scalable thermodynamic integration scheme, enhanced by machine-learning-accelerated sampling and trained on select ab initio references, can compute both solid and liquid free energies of multi-component high-entropy alloys at a fraction of the cost of fully explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, while retaining comparable accuracy in capturing vibrational and electron–vibration contributions across fusion temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys spanning up to quinary or senary compositions, initialized in equilibrium solid solution phases with partial compositional disorder.
generation.intervention: Employ parallelized nested sampling (or a similar advanced sampling technique) in tandem with a machine-learning potential periodically refined against a minimal set of ab initio calculations, covering both solid and liquid phases near melting.
generation.conditions: Temperatures from ambient to above the alloy melting range (up to approximately 2500–3000 K for refractory-based HEAs) and a broad compositional range (up to five or six principal elements).
generation.structural_mediator: Accurate interatomic forces in both solid and liquid configurations, parameterized by a machine-learned potential trained on targeted ab initio reference data.
generation.mechanism: Reducing the number of expensive on-the-fly ab initio molecular-dynamics steps by focusing ab initio sampling on representative snapshots, while progressively refining an ML-based interatomic model that captures both finite-temperature phonon-induced vibrational entropy and electron–vibration interactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: O(1–2) orders-of-magnitude throughput gain vs. ab initio MD and ~2× improvement over TOR-TILD, with free-energy and derived fusion-property predictions in near-quantitative agreement (<5–10% deviations) compared to benchmark ab initio and available experimental data.
generation.baseline: State-of-the-art ab initio molecular-dynamics approaches or TOR-TILD workflows applied to elemental and binary systems, extended to multi-component alloys with significantly higher computational cost.
generation.boundary: May be limited if strong short-range order or phase separation invalidates quasi-atomistic ML potential assumptions; strictly validated only where ab initio reference datasets sufficiently sample relevant atomic arrangements.
generation.uncertainty: Accuracy could degrade in complex high-entropy alloys with pronounced local structural distortions or magnetically ordered features if those regimes remain under-sampled in the ML potential training.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a benchmark high-entropy alloy of known multi-component composition (e.g., a refractory HEA) with measured melting range. Compute the Helmholtz free energies for solid and liquid phases over a temperature sweep, comparing advanced ML-accelerated thermodynamic integration to fully ab initio molecular-dynamics calculations (or high-fidelity TOR-TILD) and available high-temperature experimental data.
measurements: Compute free energies of both solid and liquid phases across a temperature window spanning below and above melting.
Validate each approach’s predictions of equilibrium coexistence temperature, heat of fusion, and heat capacity.
Compare predicted equilibrium phase fractions to measured or high-accuracy computational reference data.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the advanced integration plus ML approach yields fusion properties or free energies deviating by more than ~10% from the reference ab initio or experimental benchmarks, the hypothesis that this method is cost-effective without sacrificing accuracy is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: A concept for accelerated assessment of MPEAs has recently been proposed. Here we develop and apply this idea to quickly identify, screen and analyze structural alloys for use at moderate and high temperatures. We select a palette of 26 metallic elements that are most likely to produce the moderate and high-temperature properties ranges in MPEAs. The palette of elements is shown in Supplementary Table 1. Phase diagrams are the road maps for materials design, and give essential information on the phases present at a given alloy chemistry and temperature. Most binary and some ternary phase diagrams have been determined experimentally, but multi-component systems remain largely unexplored. Experimental measurement of multi-component phase diagrams is impractical due to the tremendous amount of work involved. In recent years, integration of the CALPHAD approach with key experiments has been demonstrated as an effective approach to determine complicated multi-component phase diagrams. The essence of the CALPHAD approach is to use experimental data from constituent binary and ternary phase diagrams to develop a thermodynamic database. Here, we present a preselected small set of ordered structures (PSSOS) method, a first principles-based high fidelity (HF), high throughput (HT) approach, for fast screening of the large composition space of high entropy alloys (HEAs) to select the most energetically stable, single-phase HEAs. Taking quinary AlCoCrFeNi HEA as an example system, we performed PSSOS calculations on the formation energies and mass densities of 8801 compositions in both FCC and BCC lattices and selected five most stable FCC and BCC HEAs for detailed analysis. The calculation results from the PSSOS approach were compared with existing experimental and first-principles data, and the good agreement was achieved. We also compared the PSSOS with the special quasi-random structures (SQS) method, and found that with a comparable accuracy, the PSSOS significantly outperforms the SQS in efficiency, making it ideal for HF, HT calculations of HEAs.

chosen.why: This directly addresses the slow performance of TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems by replacing its sampling bottleneck with a more efficient thermodynamic integration scheme that remains faithful to vibrational and electron–vibration contributions, as supported by existing successes in elemental and binary materials. A decisive benchmark would compare free energies and derived fusion properties computed for a known high-entropy alloy against explicit ab initio MD and experimental data, verifying both accuracy and speed improvements.
